questions.q: Corrective action means action that:
options: Fixes the problem that has occurred — this incident, this fault
Prevents an incident that has not happened
questions.explain: Corrective = fix this one. The door that failed is repaired or replaced — the incident in hand is closed.

questions.q: Preventive action means action that:
options: Stops the problem happening again or happening elsewhere — e.g. redesigning a sensor or changing a check
questions.explain: Preventive = stop the next one. It looks beyond this incident to every place the same weakness exists.

questions.q: The abbreviation CAPA, used for the pair of post-incident actions, stands for:
questions.explain: Corrective And Preventive Action (CAPA) pairs the two duties after any failure: correct what happened, prevent its return.

questions.q: Repairing the failed coach door is an example of:
questions.explain: The repair fixes the problem that occurred — that is corrective action.

questions.q: After one door sensor fails, the fleet-wide check of all similar sensors is:
options: Preventive action — the same weakness is hunted everywhere before it fails elsewhere
questions.explain: One failure is a warning for the whole fleet. Checking all similar sensors prevents the next failure.

questions.q: A complete post-incident answer names:
questions.explain: Exams love this pair: a complete answer always names both — fix it, and stop it recurring.

questions.q: An incident's root cause is found to be an unclear checklist. The strongest preventive action is:
options: Punishing the operator who used it
Filing the report and forgetting it
Rewriting the checklist step clearly and briefing all shifts on the change
questions.explain: 'Be careful' fixes nothing. Changing the system — the checklist itself — protects every future operator.

questions.q: Why is punishment generally NOT counted as a preventive action?
options: It does not remove the system weakness, so the same incident can happen to the next person
questions.explain: If the weakness stays, the incident returns with a different name attached. Prevention removes the weakness.

questions.q: A signal relay fails once and is replaced. A preventive follow-up would be:
options: Checking the age/condition of similar relays and planning their replacement before failure
Blaming the relay supplier in the report only
questions.explain: Replacement corrects; a fleet/age check of similar relays prevents the repeat performance elsewhere.

questions.q: Corrective and preventive actions should be tracked until:
options: They are actually completed and verified — an action written but not done prevents nothing
questions.explain: Corrective And Preventive Action (CAPA) lives or dies on follow-through. Actions are tracked, completed and verified, not just listed.

questions.q: After a near-miss, the most valuable preventive step is:
options: Waiting for a real incident to learn from
Forgetting it since no harm occurred
Analysing why it nearly happened and removing that weakness before it produces a real incident
questions.explain: A near-miss is a free lesson — the same incident with luck added. Analyse it like an accident, minus the damage.

questions.q: A driver reports an alarm tone that is easily confused with another alarm. The preventive action is:
options: Making the alarm tones distinctive and updating the training accordingly
questions.explain: The report exposed a system weakness. Fixing the tone protects a hundred future drivers.

questions.q: A station's escalator has broken down 4 times in 2 months, each time repaired the same day. What is still missing?
options: A preventive action — finding and removing the root cause so the repeated failure stops
questions.explain: Repeated repair is corrective action each time. When the same fault keeps returning, preventive action is missing — analyse the root cause and remove it.

questions.q: Preventive action is mainly aimed at:
options: All similar equipment, locations and situations where the same cause exists
questions.explain: Prevention thinks in classes: wherever this cause could bite again, not only where it already has.

questions.q: After corrective action, how do we know the fix worked?
options: By testing/verification — the equipment or process is checked in service before the action is closed
questions.explain: Verify the fix in service. Closing an action on paper alone is how 'fixed' faults return.

questions.q: A station's evacuation drill reveals a confusing exit sign. Corrective and preventive actions are:
options: Corrective: correct that sign now; Preventive: audit signage at all stations and fix the pattern
Corrective: punish the drill team; Preventive: cancel drills
Corrective: ignore; Preventive: more drills only
questions.explain: Fix the one sign (corrective), then hunt the same weakness at every station (preventive). Drills exist to find exactly this.

questions.q: The final step of the Corrective And Preventive Action (CAPA) cycle is:
options: Reviewing whether the actions actually prevented recurrence, and sharing the lesson
questions.explain: Review closes the loop: did it work, and who else needs the lesson? Learning unshared is learning wasted.

questions.q: An action plan lists 'staff to be more vigilant' as the only preventive action. This is weak because:
options: It changes no system, equipment or procedure — the same conditions will defeat the next person's vigilance too
questions.explain: Real prevention changes the machine, the method or the environment — not just exhorts the human.

questions.q: Lessons learned from an incident should be:
options: Kept by the enquiry team only
Shared with all relevant staff and stations, since the same weakness may exist anywhere
questions.explain: A lesson learned in one station and kept there protects one station. Shared, it protects the whole railway.

questions.q: If the same fault recurs after a 'completed' corrective action, the correct conclusion is:
options: The corrective action did not remove the real cause — re-analyse, probably to root-cause level
questions.explain: Recurrence after correction is evidence the cause was mis-identified. Go back to analysis — 5 Whys, fishbone — not to blame.

questions.q: A preventive action with the widest protection is one that:
options: Changes a design, procedure or training used by everyone
questions.explain: System-wide changes protect every shift, including the tired one at 3 a.m. Memory-based 'fixes' protect nobody reliably.

questions.q: During a live incident, the controller's focus is on containment. Corrective And Preventive Action (CAPA) belongs mainly to which phase?
options: P4 — after: restore, record, analyse and act so it does not recur
questions.explain: Corrective And Preventive Action (CAPA) is P4 work — after safety and restoration. But it must actually happen, not be forgotten once service resumes.

questions.q: Which is a preventive action after a passenger slips on a wet platform at one station?
options: A warning to passengers to walk carefully only
Anti-slip treatment and a wet-weather platform inspection routine at all stations
questions.explain: Mopping once is housekeeping; a system routine for all stations in wet weather is prevention.

questions.q: Why do examiners pair corrective and preventive action in one question?
options: Because fixing only the visible fault leaves the railway exactly as vulnerable as before — both halves complete the professional response
questions.explain: One half repairs the past, the other protects the future. A supervisor is expected to deliver both.

questions.q: A completed Corrective And Preventive Action (CAPA) should result in:
options: A measurable change — equipment, procedure, training or checks — that makes the incident less likely everywhere
questions.explain: If nothing in the system changed, nothing was prevented. Corrective And Preventive Action (CAPA) ends in change, not in paper.

questions.q: In the hierarchy of controls, which kind of preventive action is generally the STRONGEST?
options: A warning poster near the hazard
An engineering change that removes or guards the hazard itself (for example an interlock that makes the wrong action impossible)
questions.explain: Controls are strongest when they do not depend on human memory: eliminate or engineer the hazard first, then procedures, and warnings or protective equipment last.

questions.q: Every action in a Corrective And Preventive Action (CAPA) plan must carry two things, without which actions quietly die:
options: A file number and a stamp
A named owner (one responsible person) and a target completion date
A senior officer's signature and a seal
A budget code and a colour
questions.explain: 'The department will do it, sometime' means nobody will. One name and one date turn an intention into a commitment that can be tracked and chased.

questions.q: A permanent preventive fix (replacing a faulty relay type across the fleet) will take three months. For those three months, the correct supporting measure is:
options: An interim containment measure that controls the risk meanwhile — for example extra checks or a speed restriction at affected locations
Closing the line for three months
Hiding the fault from the records
questions.explain: Interim containment bridges the gap between finding a risk and finishing its cure. The permanent action removes the cause; the interim action keeps people safe till then.

questions.q: A preventive action was completed two months ago. The step that proves it actually worked is:
options: A scheduled effectiveness review — checking the incident and fault data after a set period to confirm the problem has really stopped or reduced
Asking the staff if they feel safer
questions.explain: Completion is not the same as success. The effectiveness review compares before-and-after data; if the failures continue, the action is reopened, not celebrated.

questions.q: Corrective And Preventive Action (CAPA) should be raised not only after accidents. Which set lists other proper triggers?
options: Near-misses, safety audit findings, inspection defects and drill weaknesses
Only when newspapers report a problem
questions.explain: Accidents are the costliest teachers. Audits, inspections, drills and near-misses offer the same lessons at a fraction of the price — a mature system raises Corrective And Preventive Action (CAPA) from all of them.
